title: Trent's reforms
hook: seminaries, a catechism, and a Mass book that lasted four hundred years

segments.voice: Yesterday, justification. Your line was grace first: God moves before we do. Trent wrote that down on paper. The harder question was how to get it into a parish. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

A decree is only ink until somebody carries it out. The bishops at Trent could settle grace and scripture on paper, but a village priest who had never been trained would still stand at the altar on Sunday and do what he had always done. So the council turned from doctrine to plumbing. Who teaches the priests? What book do they teach from? Which words does the Mass use? Today's word is the name that stuck to the answers: Tridentine.
screen: `INK UNTIL SOMEONE ACTS.` → `WHO TEACHES THE PRIESTS?` → `TRIDENTINE.`

segments.voice: Tridentine simply means: of Trent. It's an adjective, and it got attached to three things. First, the seminary. Trent asked each diocese to keep a college where boys and young men preparing for the priesthood would live, pray and study together, learning scripture, the sacraments and how to care for souls. The seminary made formation a place with a timetable. Second, the catechism. The council called for a book that pastors could teach from, and after it closed, one was published in Rome: the Roman Catechism, sometimes called the Catechism of the Council of Trent. It was written for priests, so that what they preached on Sunday matched what the council had taught. Third, the Missal. The council left the reform of the Mass book to the pope, and Pope Pius the Fifth issued a Roman Missal for the Latin Church. That Mass, in Latin, is what people mean today by the Tridentine Mass, and it's where today's line comes from: four hundred years. That's the round number people give for how long the book shaped the Sunday of Latin Catholics, until the reforms after the Second Vatican Council. Some Catholics still celebrate it, and the Church has set rules for when and where. Underneath all three is one idea. Jesus said, in the Douay-Rheims, "The harvest indeed is great, but the labourers are few." Trent's answer was not only to pray for laborers, but to train them.
screen: `TRIDENTINE: OF TRENT.` · `A SEMINARY IN EACH DIOCESE.` · `A CATECHISM FOR PASTORS.` · `ONE MISSAL FOR THE LATIN CHURCH.` · then, large: `FOUR HUNDRED YEARS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for seminarians. Somewhere tonight, in a seminary, young men are eating dinner, studying, wondering whether they're meant for this. For the sit, keep them in mind. If you know a seminarian, or a priest who was one, hold his face. If you pray, you can use the line Jesus gave right after the one about the harvest: "Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he send forth labourers into his harvest." If you don't pray, simply wish them good teachers. The bell holds the time.
Tridentine. Of Trent: the seminaries, the catechism and the Mass book that came out of the council. Today's word.

Your line: four hundred years. Some habits outlast the people who start them. Today, notice one thing you do because somebody trained you to, and thank them, in your head or out loud. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Catholic parishes pray for vocations, often in the Prayer of the Faithful at Mass, and dioceses keep or share a seminary where future priests live and study before ordination.

notes: The carry 'four hundred years' is fixed by the index; the voice frames it as 'the round number people give', since no cited text states the span. Keeper may prefer a different framing.
'Tridentine simply means: of Trent' is given as the adjective's meaning, not an etymology; the Latin name Tridentum is left out under the claims rule.
Confirm that the seminary decree (Session 23, ch. 18) is fairly summarized as asking each diocese to keep a college for those preparing for priesthood.
Confirm that Session 25 left the catechism and Missal to the pope, and that the Roman Catechism was addressed to parish priests.
'Some Catholics still celebrate it, and the Church has set rules for when and where' is deliberately general (current norms change); confirm wording is fair to all sides.
Years (1566 catechism, 1570 Missal, 1563 seminary decree) kept out of the voice under the claims rule.
